messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Conflict: Confrontations, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event

Vignette:
Mark is a 49-year-old married plumber who came to treatment after months of telling himself that what happened was over and that he should be able to get on with things. The assault had taken place during the end of a relationship before his current marriage, in a house where he had been living with a romantic partner whose anger had become increasingly unpredictable. One night an argument began in the kitchen and escalated quickly. He remembers the smell first as much as anything else: something burning on the stove, sharp and acrid, spreading through the room while his partner raised her voice and moved toward him. In his account, the details of the fight are tied tightly to that sensory atmosphere—the hot kitchen, the burnt smell, the sense that there was nowhere easy to go. When he tried to disengage, she struck him. What stayed with him was not only the physical force but the moment of being cornered while someone he was close to looked furious and kept coming at him.

In the weeks afterward, Mark did not talk much about the assault. He returned to work, kept up his plumbing calls, and tried to put practical distance between himself and the apartment where it happened. He had come to believe that thinking about that night was dangerous in itself, as if giving it any room in his mind would pull him back into the same helplessness he had felt in the kitchen. When the memory began to edge in, he would interrupt it quickly, turn on the television, scroll on his phone, or find some task to keep his hands occupied. He described doing this almost automatically, as though he could feel the thought approaching and had to shut the door before it fully arrived.

His evenings changed first. Sleep became something he delayed rather than entered. He would stay up very late, sitting in front of the television long after his wife had gone to bed, telling himself he was not tired yet or that he needed to unwind. More privately, he knew that going to sleep meant being still, and being still meant there was less to distract him from the kitchen, the shouting, and the smell of something scorching on the stove. Night after night, he kept himself awake until he was exhausted enough to drop off quickly.

In daily life, reminders appeared in ways that made sense to him but left him feeling hemmed in. A burnt smell could catch him immediately. On plumbing jobs he sometimes entered homes where a pan had been left too long on a burner or a garbage disposal motor had overheated, and the odor would hit him before he had even set his toolbox down. In those moments he felt his body tense and his mind narrow to the scene around him. He would become intent on locating exits, finishing fast, or stepping outside under the pretense of getting something from the truck. Conflict of any kind also began to feel loaded. If a customer confronted him about cost or timing, or if someone’s tone sharpened during a disagreement, Mark found himself bracing as if something worse were about to happen. What unsettled him most was that even calm expressions of anger in other people could do it. A set jaw, clipped words, a spouse irritated with a contractor in the next room—none of it had to be loud for him to feel on edge.

Over time he also organized his life around not going near the place where the assault had happened. He would take different routes to avoid that block, and if a work call came in nearby, he tried to trade it away or invent another reason not to go. This had practical consequences. He lost convenient jobs and added time to his days to steer clear of that area. At home, his wife noticed how stubbornly he avoided certain parts of town and how late he stayed up, but Mark struggled to explain it. He did not want to revisit the event out loud, and he especially did not want to be seen as a man who had let this continue to shape him.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing. He was tired, irritable, and increasingly aware that ordinary encounters at work could leave him shaken for hours. What finally brought him in was a recent plumbing job in a home where dinner had burned on the stove while the owners argued in the next room. The smell and the tension together were enough that he had to step outside and sit in his van until he could steady himself. He found that frightening not because he lacked words for it, but because he could see how much of his life had quietly narrowed. He says he wants help so he can sleep normally and stop arranging his routes, jobs, and evenings around that night. What he is most afraid of is that if he lets himself think about the assault directly, it will feel as immediate as ever. What he most hopes is that it can finally become something that happened, rather than something waiting around corners in other people’s voices and in the smell of something burnt.
